turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you're chief product officer at Wise, which I don't know if you knew this, but I'm a very happy weekly active user of. To give folks a little bit of context on Wise, could you just explain, what does Wise do? And also share maybe a few stats to give people a sense of the scale that Wise has reached at this point.
turns.zh: 您现在是Wise的首席产品官，我不知道您是否了解，但我每周都非常活跃地使用Wise这款产品。先给听众简单介绍一下Wise吧——Wise是做什么的？或许您可以分享一些数据，让大家了解Wise目前的规模。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: We're looking to solve the problems associated with cross-border money movement, which is that moving money across border is pretty slow. It's actually really expensive, and it can be really hard to do. We solve it with three products, our money transfer product, which is what we started with, our account, which would be like, think of trying to solve the problems of international banking with our account for people, and for businesses. And then finally we've also got an enterprise product where we take the underlying infrastructure that's powered those products that we've built, and embed them in the banks, and products that people use every day, and then zooming into the numbers. So, we've got to come a little way on the journey. So today we're now moving about $12 billion a month, growing between 30 to 40% year on year. We take about 0.65% on average across all our routes as price, and we've been profitable for about more than four years now, with 20% EBITDA margins. (00:05:05): But probably the stat I'm most proud of, and the hardest thing to make happen out of all of that was we acquired 70% of the users that found out about Wise last month through word of mouth. So, contextually, we have 16 million customers, and we're acquiring about a million a quarter, about 10 million actives, and yes, so out of a million that joined Wise the first time, 700,000 found out about Wise from a friend.
turns.zh: 我们致力于解决跨境资金转移的难题。跨境转账速度缓慢、费用高昂且操作复杂。我们通过三款产品来实现这一目标：首先是我们最初推出的转账产品；其次是Wise账户产品，旨在为个人和企业解决国际银行服务难题；最后，我们还开发了企业级产品，将底层基础设施嵌入银行和日常使用的应用中。具体数据方面，目前我们每月处理约120亿美元的转账业务，年同比增长30%至40%。我们所有路径的平均收费率为0.65%，且已实现盈利四年多，EBITDA利润率达20%。（00:05:05）最令我自豪、同时也是最难实现的数据是，上个月通过口口相传了解Wise的用户中，70%最终成为了我们的付费用户。Wise目前拥有1600万客户，每季度新增约100万用户，其中约1000万为活跃用户。值得一提的是，首次使用Wise的用户中，有70万人是通过朋友推荐发现Wise的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple stats there that really stand out to me. One is you're gaining a million new users a quarter, which is insane. Just like a million new people joining Wise every quarter. That's an astounding number. The other number is what you just shared around word of mouth, that basically more than two thirds of people are discovering Wise and joining Wise through word of mouth. Mouth. I want to spend the bulk of our conversation on this topic of word of mouth. I think it's extremely rare how you've been able to increase word of mouth, and just how much of your growth comes through word of mouth. (00:06:08): You've essentially developed a system for how to drive word of mouth, and how to basically structure your team, your goals, your priorities and things like that in order to lean into this growth channel. And so, I just have a million questions around how you think about word of mouth, and the first is just, how do you measure word of mouth? How do you know that say, 70% of your growth is coming through word of mouth?
turns.zh: 有几个数据点让我印象深刻。首先，每季度新增100万用户，这数字太惊人了。每季度都有100万新用户加入Wise，真是难以置信。其次，关于口口相传的数据——超过三分之二的新用户是通过朋友推荐发现并加入Wise的。我想我们今天主要探讨口口相传的话题。我认为你们能如此有效地提升口口相传效果，如此依赖这一增长渠道，这实在是难能可贵。（00:06:08）你们显然开发了一套驱动口口相传的系统，包括构建团队目标、优先级等机制。关于口口相传，我有几个问题想深入探讨。首先，如何衡量口口相传的效果？如何确认70%的增长来自口口相传？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: We ask customers, is the short answer. So, we have an attribution model, as you can imagine, and we've had one from the early days, and it overlays all the referrer data and cookie data you have on visits comes to the website. So you kind of know that. And then you obviously have the soundtrack stuff, and we sample, and ask customers a set of questions on this, and then overlay that onto the... What turns up in your web tracking as direct traffic to give us a sense of how big that word of mouth number is, and that's what gets us back to the 70% stat.
turns.zh: 简单来说，我们会直接询问用户。实际上，我们从早期就建立了归因模型，将推荐数据和cookie数据叠加到网站访问数据中。这样就能准确衡量口口相传的效果，再结合网站追踪数据中的直接访问量，最终得出70%的口口相传数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And very practically, how do you actually ask people? Is there a little pop-up on the website?
turns.zh: 实际上，具体该怎么问用户呢？网站上会有弹窗提示吗？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: It's actually integrated into the flow. So when we built it originally, we thought it's quite cool, marketing and acquiring customers is part of the product, and we should actually stitch that into the experience seamlessly so that we're able to do this more effectively going forward.
turns.zh: 这个功能其实是嵌入到整个用户体验流程中的。最初开发时，我们觉得这很棒——营销和用户获取是产品的重要组成部分，应该将其无缝融入到用户体验中，以便未来能更高效地实现这些目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's actually, at Airbnb, exactly how the team did that, to understand what percentage of growth was word of mouth. It's just a little interstitial popup when you visit say, airbnb.com, "How'd you hear about us?" You think there's some fancy ways to understand the stuff, but it's just like, just ask people, they'll tell you how they heard about it.
turns.zh: 在Airbnb，团队就是这么做的，通过分析口碑传播的比例。当用户访问airbnb.com时，会弹出一个简短的提示：“你是如何得知我们的？”你可能以为有复杂的分析方法，但其实答案很简单——直接问用户，他们会告诉你他们是如何得知的。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so just to kind of dig into the meat of it, what has been the biggest shift in helping you significantly grow word of mouth, and make it such a huge lever of growth for Wise?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来深入探讨一下：在帮助Wise显著提升口碑传播方面，最重大的转变是什么？口碑传播为何能成为Wise增长的关键驱动力？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, before I launch into this, let's just also take a step back, and why even focus on this? So in the early days, when I met the founders, Kristo and Tyler. It was quite funny, I got introed to them when they were just the founders, and without a team really, and with the beginnings of a product, and they said, "Nilan, you've got to meet these guys, they've got a great product, they just don't have any customers." And I sat there with them, and we kind of launched the first Google ads, and in the early days you try everything, hoping that something works. But taking a step back, think of money as the ultimate commodity. It's pretty hard to build an expensive business that moves your money somewhere, and it costs a lot, so there's less of it afterwards. (00:08:48): So building a brand led money transfer business, the brand's got to be pretty damn good, right? You're going to feel pretty special afterwards, in order to have less money afterwards. So what we're looking for always, but what channels out there are super scalable, and can reach our entire audience, but have an incredibly low distribution cost. So, that's one thing that led us to word of mouth and the other bit, when we get on to talk about marketing later, the other challenge with marketing which is unique is because we are lower price, but a superior product, we have less margin to spend on marketing than others in certain paid channels. So that's another reason why marketing is inherently hard. Our marketing team does amazing work at Wise, in order to work within those constraints. (00:09:36): But back to your question, which was like, what's the biggest thing we've done to shift word of mouth. When I joined Wise, and started wrangling with word of mouth, I spent a bunch of time with friends of mine in the US and around the world, Andrew Chen, some of the other growth gurus, this is going back 10, 12 years. It's like what mouths, who's done it? What's the system? What do you measure? There wasn't really anything out there. So we kind of had to figure our way out. So, first step was asking it, and the second step was kind of figure out how do you know what's driving it? And the best proxy we found for this was something that most people have heard of, that we actually used quite a lot is net promoter score. (00:10:26): So from the very early days we'd start asking customers, and you probably have seen this survey, "Would you recommend Wise to a friend?"
turns.zh: 是啊，在我深入讲解之前，先退一步想想：为什么要关注这个问题呢？早在公司创立初期，我结识了创始人克里斯托（Kristo）和泰勒（Tyler）。说起来挺有趣的，当时他们还是初创团队，产品尚在雏形阶段，就有人向我推荐他们：“尼兰（Nilan），你一定要认识这俩人，他们产品很棒，但现在还没客户。”于是我和他们坐下来，共同推出首款谷歌广告服务。早期阶段，你会尝试各种方法，希望其中一种能奏效。但退一步想，钱是终极商品。打造一个能让资金流转的昂贵业务实在不易，成本高昂，投入后可用资金反而减少了。（00:08:48）所以打造品牌化的转账业务，品牌必须足够出色，对吧？你得先觉得自己很特别，才能在后期牺牲资金。另一方面，我们一直在寻找高效可扩展的渠道，要能触达所有用户，同时分销成本极低。这也是我们选择口碑传播的原因。再说营销挑战——因为我们的产品价格更低，但质量更高，相比其他付费渠道，我们能投入的营销资金更少。这也是营销天然难做的原因。Wise的营销团队在这些限制条件下做得很棒。（00:09:36）回到你的问题：我们为提升口碑做了哪些最大努力？加入Wise后，当我开始攻克口碑难题时，我花了大量时间与美国及全球的朋友交流，比如安德鲁·陈（Andrew Chen）等增长专家，这可以追溯到10、12年前。我们探讨：口碑如何形成？谁做得好？衡量标准是什么？当时几乎没有现成方案。所以我们只能自己摸索。第一步是提出问题，第二步是分析驱动因素。我们发现一个大家耳熟能详的指标——净推荐值（NPS），这正是我们大量应用的工具。（00:10:26）从早期开始，我们就开始询问客户：“你会向朋友推荐Wise吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Never seen that ever in my life. Never been asked that question.
turns.zh: 我这辈子从没见过这种调查。也从没被问过这个问题。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Exactly. There's [inaudible 00:10:41] you said. And then in the end you've got the scale, zero to 10, and the theory is nine to 10 there are promoters, and zero to seven are detractors. Zero to six, detractors, and seven to eight are kind of neutral on your product. The intriguing bet was when we overlaid this... So we have word of mouth, it's about 50 odd percent, and then we have a referral program. When we overlay the referral data over the NPS survey data, we saw something really interesting. (00:11:13): There's very low invite rates at one to six, and not just invite, conversion rates of users that joined for invites. But when we've got people from sixes to this seven and eight group, they doubled the number of people they told. Eight to nine, they doubled again, and nine to 10, they doubled again. So, this is pretty crazy when you see it for the first time. I'm going to get back to your question in a sec, but it's quite core buildup to it, because when you are a product manager, like you've been in your career, one of your jobs is to figure out what metric are you going to optimize for? What are you going to try to get the business to ground behind? And if you optimize for something like conversion, rate and you move conversion rate with 10%, you kind of get this one-off hit. (00:12:00): But if you move the NPS from 30% to 50%, you increase the viral coefficient of your customer base. So every customer that goes through tells X many more. When you model this through, the ROI on NPS increases is absolutely huge. So, it's got to say, "Okay, this is the thing to zoom in on, so how to move it?" So, then the second magic of NPS is you get the numbers, but you also get the comments underneath it. I remember in the first year we built the NPS survey, and we emailed out every week all the comments to the whole company, which was pretty small, and we kept doing that, I think up till about three or four years, everyone got the NPS comments. (00:12:51): And when you read the comments, and now obviously we've got all kinds of fancy models sitting on top of these things, customers kept telling us the same things, "Make it faster, make it cheaper, make it easier to use." Do you know at the beginning, when I said, "Price, speed, ease of use," we kind of figured this out by thinking hard about this question. How do we make this product so good that people will use, it but they'll recommend it? (00:13:20): And customers were pretty clear, the ones that were evangelical, is the word we use, are the ones that had a much... Had this cheaper experience, the ones that were talking about it had a fast experience. So it's about price, about speed, it's about ease of use. And when you generalize and take a step back, and look at consumer product companies, they have these product pillars they call it, and they usually have KPIs around them. The second insight we got, found, is when we entered markets, like when we entered the US for the first time, if we entered with a product that was priced at say 5.9%, and the alternative was six, customers would use us, but they wouldn't talk about us. We only got the advocacy when we were eight to 10 times cheaper. That's when people started talking about it.
turns.zh:
没错。你提到的就是这个。最后我们还引入了NPS（净推荐值）评分体系，分值范围是0到10。根据理论，分值在9到10的用户是忠实拥趸，0到7的则属于不满群体。0到6分的用户属于不满群体，而7到8分的用户对产品持中立态度。最有趣的发现是，当我们将口碑数据与NPS调查数据叠加分析时（00:11:13），发现邀请率在1到6分时极低，不仅邀请率低，接受邀请加入的用户转化率也很低。但当邀请率达到7到8分时，用户推荐人数翻倍，8到9分时再翻倍，9到10分时再次翻倍。这真是令人惊叹的发现。

（00:12:00）回到你的问题。这是核心分析部分。作为产品经理，你的职责之一就是确定优化指标，争取让业务团队支持。若优化转化率，提升10%，可能只是短暂的提升。但若将NPS从30%提升至50%，客户群体的病毒式传播系数会大幅提升。每个用户都会口口相传。通过模型分析，NPS带来的ROI回报极其可观。因此必须聚焦于此，思考如何提升NPS。

（00:12:51）NPS的第二个魔力在于数据背后的用户反馈。我记得第一年我们推出NPS调查时，每周向全体员工（当时公司规模不大）发送用户反馈邮件，并持续了三四年。阅读这些反馈时，我们发现用户不断重复三个关键诉求：速度、价格、易用性。最初我们提出的三大核心诉求——价格、速度、易用性，正是通过深入思考后总结出来的。

（00:13:20）用户口碑的核心是性价比。那些热情推荐的用户，无不经历过更低价格、更快体验的转变。归纳来看，无论是消费品公司还是科技产品，都有其核心产品支柱，并围绕其制定KPI。我们在美国市场扩张时发现，当产品定价5.9%（替代方案6美元）时，用户会使用但不会推荐。只有当价格降至8到10倍时，用户才会主动推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me actually interrupt you here a bit, just to kind of set a little frame around this, because this is extremely interesting, and I think people may miss, I think, some of the really interesting insights here. What I'm hearing is essentially there's this clear sense that you had to grow through word of mouth because of the business model. You didn't make a lot of money per user, and you didn't have a lot of money to spend thus, to help grow. So essentially it's like. "How do we grow the word of mouth?" And then it's, "Okay, what do we need to convince people to share this product?" And used NPS, which I think a lot of people use, and also a lot of people probably know, "Let's make our product more awesome so that people talk about it." Those are kind of like, "Oh yeah, of course." (00:14:49): But I think what I'm hearing is that you did that's really unique, is one, you found this huge delta between these detractors, and even seven or... I guess it was six and below, and then seven or eight, and then nine, 10 kept kind of doubling. So one is just this focus on, how do we get someone from there to there? Two is this really big focus on the comments of the NPS survey, not just like, "Oh we have this percentage of detractors." And then also I love how you just create these pillars, essentially, of like, "We're going to work on these three things. These are the three levers to help grow word of mouth for this product." Does that sound about right?
turns.zh: 容我先插句话，稍微理一下思路，因为这事儿挺有意思的，我觉得大家可能会忽略一些关键洞察。我听到的核心观点是，鉴于当时的商业模式，你们不得不靠口口相传来发展用户基础。每个用户的收益微薄，也没有太多资金投入推广，所以核心问题就是："如何激发口碑传播？"然后是"如何说服用户分享产品？"你们用了NPS（净推荐值），我相信很多人都用过，也很熟悉这个指标——"让产品更吸引人，让用户主动传播"。但我觉得你们的做法很独特：首先，发现了用户评分的巨大鸿沟，从7分以下的差评群体，到7、8分的中评群体，再到9、10分的推荐群体，增长呈指数级攀升。其次，高度重视NPS调查中的用户反馈，不只是看"差评比例"，而是深入解读用户评论。还有，你们构建了三大核心策略支柱——专注于这三个关键点，驱动产品口碑增长。这听起来很对吧？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: That all makes sense. Obviously at the time, it is also way more chaotic.
turns.zh: 这都说得通。显然当时的环境要混乱得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: So, at the beginning, everyone thinks it's 20 different things, and then over time, slowly, you understand that it's these things again and again. And a lot of building a successful businesses kind of building conviction that these are the things that matter. So, now I'd say price, speed, ease of use, it sounds... Like, but yeah, go back to seven, eight years. But we were arguing with each other around what, "Is it trust? Is it this? Is it this?" Trying to get clear on what are the things we missed there.
turns.zh: 刚开始大家觉得有20个不同的方向，后来慢慢发现其实都是这些要素。打造成功的商业模式，关键在于形成共识，确定哪些才是真正重要的。比如现在我会说，价格、速度、易用性，这些听起来很基础，但回到七八年前，我们还在纠结“是信任吗？是这个吗？还是那个？”，试图理清那些被忽视的关键点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That would be useful actually to know. It sounds like, of course, it's going to be price and speed, but what are the things you kind of realize you don't need to focus on as much, based on these surveys?
turns.zh: 这确实很有参考价值。听起来价格和速度是必备的，但基于这些调查，你们发现哪些方面可以适当放缓关注？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Oh, wow, that's a really hard one. So, then the challenge, is as you know, everything is important.
turns.zh: 哦，哇，这确实是个难题。毕竟所有因素都重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah? And that things that we use... We have a bucket called convenience. And inside the convenience bucket, there are many, many things hiding in there. And actually, you can measure this on contact rate, conversion rate, whatever, many different ways, and get many slightly different answers. So, I think I've learned there isn't... I haven't got a good answer on things we haven't-
turns.zh: 是吗？我们常用的指标……我们有个叫“便利性”的维度，其中包含很多子项。实际上，可以通过接触率、转化率等多种维度衡量，得到不同结论。所以我觉得我还没找到通用的答案……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, as you said, trust, which is interesting. Obviously trust matters, but maybe it sounds like-
turns.zh: 嗯，正如你提到的，信任很重要。这没错，但听起来……

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Trust certainly matters. Yeah, trust's a good one. Let's talk about that one bit. I'll talk to you through the trust problem. So I ran into the trust problem hardest in marketing. So, just imagine, you just started out, you've got a money transfer company, it's good, your product's really good, it's really cheap. So, you put an ad out, and it says, "Move money with Wise, and really cheaply," is anyone going to click that? People did, right? Is anyone going to use it? Yeah, people did use it. And you did work all the usual trust elements. But the bit I found that really helped, the way I got my head around this, was what people trust is their friends. And this really was way stronger a trust signal than anything I could put on a landing page. (00:17:40): And even when people came in through marketing, they'd been told. So marketing can aid recall, and all kinds of things, because people are told by their friends. They'd have a use case later on, then Google, and like, "Ah, I remember, this guy used this." And we do definitely get users, especially today as we've got a larger brand, through marketing direct. But trust in isolation is a really hard problem to solve. You need to get under the skin of what it means. People don't think my money is safe. "I don't know if this company is reputable," to unpick each of these problems and figure out systemically how to solve them. And we've done this to some extent, but really there's a massive shortcut, which is if you deliver your customers a good experience, then figure out, how do you make it so good they'll recommend it? Then that kind of shortcut a lot of really hard trust problems.
turns.zh: 信任无疑至关重要。是啊，信任是个很重要的话题。咱们就来深入探讨一下。我会跟大家讲讲信任方面的问题。我在营销领域遇到的信任难题最为深刻。想象一下，你刚起步，经营一家汇款公司，产品质量不错，收费也很亲民。于是你投放广告，写着“用Wise汇款，超低价”，会有人点击吗？确实有人点击了。但用户会实际使用吗？当然有用过。不过我发现最有效的解决办法，是让人们相信自己的朋友。这种信任信号远比我在登陆页面上设置的任何机制都更有说服力。（00:17:40）即便用户是通过营销渠道引流的，他们也是被朋友推荐的。人们会记住使用案例，之后再去谷歌搜索时会想：“啊，我记得这家公司靠谱。”如今我们品牌规模更大了，确实能通过直效营销直接获取用户。但单纯靠信任来解决问题实在太难了。你得深入理解信任的本质。比如用户会担心钱款安全，质疑公司信誉，这些问题都需要拆解，系统性地寻找解决方案。我们在一定程度上做到了，但其实有个捷径，那就是提供优质的客户体验，然后想办法让用户主动推荐。这就能省去很多复杂的信任难题了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What did you find most helped increase trust in that way? Is it just get more people using it and then they'll share with their friends, or is there something you did there to...
turns.zh: 你觉得哪种方法最有效地提升了信任？是先让更多人使用产品，然后他们会主动分享，还是说你采取了某些特定措施...

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: No, it was literally get more people using it, and they'll share with their friends. There's obviously a bunch of learnings we've had around what specific trust sentiments matter, especially geographically, but less powerful in the macro than get more people to use it. (00:18:52): So coming back to that, and I'd love to get your thoughts on this one. So, as you said, lots of people go up to NPS, and they kind of heard people talk about it, heard people talk about recommendations. So my learning on this is you've got to work really hard to get recommendation. So, to get a nine or a 10, so our NPS is 70%, so it's really, really high. So it's kind of higher than the iPhone, and Google search. So really, really high, so off the scale high. (00:19:25): And when we launch a market, or at the beginning it was much lower, so 20s and 30s. So instead it in context, like banks and financial services NPS is -30. So, most people don't recommend banks. So it's like, comes from a low base. But, what I've found is when you build a product, most founders, and most teams kind of stop when it works. As their next step, some people focus on conversion rate like, "I'm going to make this really, really slick," and that's cool, you get a bit more growth. (00:20:02): But to get to recommendation, you're going to blow your users' socks off, and the phrase we use is, you have to give them an experience they didn't know was previously possible. And when you are in that place of doing something that no one has ever done before, that's where you get it. (00:20:24): So the bar is all the way up there. And to put that in context, that means figuring out how to move money instantly. That means figuring out how to drop the price all the way from six all the way down to 0.35. And that's because there are systemic infrastructure issues in moving money around the world, which some people haven't solved before. And these problems are just really hard to solve. They take years to solve, but they have huge kind of returns when you do it.
turns.zh: 不是的，实际上就是让更多的人使用它，然后他们会把它分享给朋友。我们当然从中总结了不少经验，比如哪些特定的信任因素很重要，尤其是地域因素，但这些因素在宏观层面的影响远不如让更多人使用它来得大。（00:18:52）：回到这个问题，我很想听听你的看法。正如你所说，很多人都提到NPS，他们听别人谈论过推荐机制。所以我的体会是，你必须下很大功夫才能获得推荐。比如，要达到9分或10分，我们的NPS是70%，已经非常高了。这甚至比iPhone和谷歌搜索的评分还要高，可以说高得离谱。（00:19:25）：当我们在某个市场推出产品时，起初评分很低，比如二三十分。相比之下，银行和金融服务业的NPS通常是-30，说明大多数人不愿意推荐银行。所以这是从低起点起步的。但我发现，当你开发产品时，大多数创始人和团队在产品成功后往往就停下了。有些人会专注于转化率，比如“我要把产品做得超级流畅”，这固然能带来一些增长。（00:20:02）：但要获得推荐，你必须给用户带来惊喜。我们常说，你得给他们一种前所未有的体验。当你能做到前所未有的创新时，推荐自然而然就会产生。（00:20:24）：所以标准非常高。我举个例子，比如即时转账功能。这意味着要解决全球资金流动的系统性问题，之前没人能做到。而这些问题又极难解决，往往需要数年时间才能突破，但一旦成功，回报将是巨大的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that just as a framework, is how do... We need to blow our users' socks off. And again, it just comes back to how you can get people to want to share this product, and drive word of mouth, blow their socks off. (00:21:02): I want to dig into how you actually just figured out what these attributes are. Obviously you talked about this NPS survey highlighting things. How did you decide it was instant money movement, and some of the other things? Is it just basically looking at these survey results, and picking the things that come up most often?
turns.zh: 我觉得这作为一个框架很棒，就是如何……我们必须给用户带来惊喜。再说回来，关键在于如何让人们愿意分享产品，推动口碑传播，让他们惊叹不已。（00:21:02）：我想深入探讨一下，你们是如何确定这些关键属性的。显然，你们通过NPS调查找到了重点。你们是如何确定即时转账功能和其他要素的？是不是主要通过分析调查结果，挑选出出现频率最高的点？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, it was talking to customers, and looking at the survey results, and then through that, in many different ways, price will come up, speed will come up, ease of use will come up, and they kind of aggregate up to that.
turns.zh: 是的，我们通过与客户沟通，分析调查结果，最终总结出价格、速度、易用性等因素，这些因素汇聚成最终的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think a lot of people listening are still going to be this like, "Okay, we're just going to make our product awesome, and it's going to grow." And in a sense, yeah, in another sense what you're sharing is essentially kind of a really simple framework for how to actually do that. To kind of go a little deeper there, when you see other people trying to drive word of mouth, trying to drive virality, is there anything you think people often do wrong? Is there other missteps you've taken in trying to drive word of mouth?
turns.zh: 我觉得很多听众可能还是会想，“好吧，我们只要把产品做得超棒，用户自然会增长。” 从某种意义上说，是的。但从另一个角度看，你分享的其实是一个如何实现增长的简单框架。再深入一点，当你看到其他人试图推动口碑传播、实现病毒式增长时，你认为他们常犯哪些错误？在推动口碑传播方面，你们有没有踩过哪些雷？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: It's this thing around growth rate. So, especially product net growth, which is what we're talking about. So you can imagine, we're going to open a new market to Indonesia, and the fastest way to do it is to take... Someone else has figured out how to move to Indonesia. We take that infrastructure, and we'll plug it into Wise, (00:22:18): You know what? We can do this, we'll get some users. But it doesn't grow like a hockey stick. It doesn't grow like a hockey stick because we haven't fundamentally changed the problems in moving money internationally. So, got this mantra, you've got to build a 10x better product than what's there. And if it's 10x product better, basically it doesn't exist already. So if you're plugging in something else, that's kind of a misstep. (00:22:45): So it comes from a very logical place, how do I get users quickly? I can take a shortcut in doing this, but that, you kind of realize is wasted effort. So the step then becomes this much harder question of these types of questions. Like what is the theoretical minimum cost for moving money into a market? What is the theoretical maximum speed? Not just make it instant, make it cheap, but what actually is the lowest it could possibly be? And instead of incrementally going, doing a jump to make it a little better, a little better, a little better, you can never get there. How do we take two years, and end up there?
turns.zh: 关键在于增长率的问题。特别是产品净增长率，也就是我们今天要讨论的重点。想象一下，我们要开拓印度尼西亚市场，最快的办法就是借鉴别人的成功经验。（00:22:18）：你知道吗？我们可以复制现有的模式，吸引一些用户，但增长不会像曲棍球棒一样直线上升。这是因为我们尚未从根本上解决跨境转账的难题。因此，我们需要遵循一个原则：产品必须比现有同类产品好十倍。但如果只是简单地复制别人的模式，那就走错路了。（00:22:45）：所以问题源于一个合理的逻辑：如何快速获取用户？我们可以走捷径，但很快就会发现这是徒劳的。因此，挑战就升级到更深层的问题，比如：将资金引入新市场的理论最低成本是多少？理论最大速度又有多快？不只是追求即时性，还要追求低成本。答案是什么？而不是逐步改进，永远达不到目标。如何用两年时间实现目标？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. It's something that I talk about a lot. Something I learned at Airbnb is this idea of working backwards from the ideal, instead of working forwards from how do we iterate and make this better, and better, and better. It's like, okay, if we could start again, and we could create the ideal experience, what would that look like? And then work backwards from what would it take to get there?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这种思维方式。这也是我在Airbnb学到的重要理念——从理想状态倒推，而不是从如何迭代优化中前进。就像是，如果能重新开始，打造理想体验会是什么样子？然后倒推实现这个目标需要哪些条件？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: And what's an example of that at Airbnb? What was an ideal that you guys went for and then built?
turns.zh: Airbnb的一个例子是什么？你们当时追求的理想是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The ideal was, there's this whole process where the founders hired this storyboard artist from Pixar to draw out the ideal experience of a host and a guest. So, there's these storyboards sitting in the office. I think there's 12 kind of... They call them key frames of, it's just like the booking experience being really seamless, arriving in the home, and being really amazed. Going out and finding things to do. (00:24:13): So, this became essentially the vision of the company is let's make each of these frames, these key moments of a journey for hosting a guest as incredible as possible. That was one, and that became essentially the strategy for a few years is just make each of these frames awesome. (00:24:29): And then there was another project that they were working on around booking at Airbnb. I don't know if you remember this, if you used Airbnb much, but most of Airbnb back in the day was you request to book with a host, you're like, "Hey, can I stay in your home?"
turns.zh: 理想状态是，创始人聘请了皮克斯的故事情节设计师，绘制出房东和房客的理想体验流程图。办公室里至今还挂着12幅这样的关键帧图，完美呈现了从预订到入住，再到探索周边的无缝体验。（00:24:13）：于是公司的愿景就定下来：让旅程中的每个关键时刻都尽可能完美。随后几年策略就是专注于打造每个完美场景。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And turned out 50% of the time the guest was ignored, or rejected, and the host was just like, "Nah, no thank you." Now, over 80% as far as I know of bookings are instant bookings, where you just book and it's done, just like every other place you book online. And so that was a huge transition that I worked on, and that came from, if we were to start Airbnb again today, or if someone were to disrupt Airbnb, what would it look like? And obviously it'd be you just book. You're not sitting around hoping someone is cool with you. So, that came from that idea of just like, what would be the ideal Airbnb experience?
turns.zh: 结果发现，50%的情况下客人被忽视或拒绝，房东往往会说：“不了，谢谢。”据我所知，如今超过80%的预订都是即时预订——你只需预订即可完成交易，就像在其他在线预订平台一样。这是我致力于推动的一项重大变革。假如我们今天重新创办Airbnb，或者有人想颠覆Airbnb，它会是什么样子？显然，用户只需直接预订即可，无需等待房东回复。所以这一切都源于这样一个理念：理想的Airbnb体验应该是什么样的？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: That is incredibly inspiring. I'll try and share a couple of stories, analogies from Wise. I'll talk about two things. Let's talk about price first. So, it's a good question. So, Moneytrans has been around since the [inaudible 00:25:32]. How does a few people get together? And it's evolved towards moving trillions around the world, and generally retail consumers paying about six to 7% around the world to do it. How do a small team in Europe start out and figure out how to move it? We launched at 0.5%, and now we're down to about 0.35%. So what changed?
turns.zh: 这真是太鼓舞人心了。我会试着分享几个故事，以及来自Wise的类比。我想谈谈两个方面。首先是价格问题。这是个好问题。Moneytrans自[00:25:32未听清]以来就一直存在。几个人如何聚集在一起？它逐渐发展为全球数万亿美元的转账业务，全球零售消费者为此平均支付6%至7%的费用。那么，一支欧洲小团队如何起步并找到转账的解决方案？我们最初的费率是0.5%，现在已降至约0.35%。那么发生了什么变化呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was going to ask, how did you do that? That sounds like everyone would want to do that.
turns.zh: 是的，我正想问，你们是如何做到的？听起来这似乎是每个人都想做的。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, so let's try to unpick it a little bit. So, first question you'd ask is, "I know what you're doing, you're losing money on every transfer." It's like, "Especially what you're doing," but we've been profitable for five years. And one of the magical things here was we're actually profitable in every transaction. So it's probably about four or five years ago, I led this project to start to pull together our pricing. (00:26:30): So, every month you get bills, and they turn up in your P&L, but every single bill we got, we allocated the cost back to the customer, or the transaction that generated it. And then we add our margin on top, and that's our price. And when you look at this and you analyze it, you'll find obviously there are 20% of customers generating 80% of the costs. And what you do is you get those 20%, you give them a raise, because they should cover their costs, and you drop the price to everyone else. And then the team works really hard on reducing these costs down, and then you move into a different segment in the market as the price costs come down. Does that make sense, Lenny?
turns.zh: 是的，让我们试着仔细分析一下。首先你会问：“我知道你们在做什么，每次转账都会亏损。” 确实如此，但我们已经盈利五年了。这里有个神奇之处，我们每笔交易实际上都是盈利的。大约四五年前，我领导了一个项目，开始整合我们的定价策略。（00:26:30）：每个月你都会收到账单，这些账单会出现在损益表中，但我们收到的每笔账单，我们都会将成本分摊回给产生它的客户或交易。然后我们再加上我们的利润，这就是我们的价格。当你分析这一切时，你会发现显然有20%的客户产生了80%的成本。那么你要做的就是提高这20%的价格，因为他们应该承担自己的成本，然后将价格降低给其他人。然后团队会努力降低这些成本，随着价格下降，再进入市场的不同细分领域。这说得通吗，Lenny？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Essentially charge the heavier users more to counteract less frequent users. And essentially that drives word of mouth.
turns.zh: 是的。本质上，就是向高频用户收取更多费用，以抵消低频用户的成本。这样就能推动口碑传播。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Totally, but it's down to this level of, if an Australian customer calls up asking, "Where is my transfer?" That cost of that call gets allocated back to the AUD/GBP route. If a Brazilian business needs like 20 documents in order to be verified before we can give them an account, the cost of verifying check those customers goes back there, so that at a very atomic level starts happening. So yeah, as you said, the more expensive customers end up paying what they cost.
turns.zh: 完全正确，但具体到每个层面，如果一位澳大利亚客户打电话问：“我的转账在哪里？” 这通电话的成本会被分摊回AUD/GBP路线。如果一家巴西企业需要20份文件才能验证，然后才能给他们一个账户，验证这些客户的成本也会被分摊回去。这样，在非常细微的层面上，这种情况就会发生。所以是的，正如你所说，更昂贵的市场最终会让客户支付更高的价格。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it sounds like the more expensive markets.
turns.zh: 而且听起来似乎是更昂贵的市场。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Indeed, and the more expensive, systemically expensive markets. But let's get to that. So, what are the costs? So if you look at our P&L, there's just three costs at transaction level. You've got people costs, you've got the cost of risk, realized risk, and then you've got partner fees. (00:28:16): And so if you've got this mission of moving the world's money for almost nothing, or zero, as close to zero as you can, you've got to invest as much of your cashflow in engineering to try to engineer away these three problems. So just to take them through briefly a bit, and remember, we're trying to do this 10 times better than anyone else. So how do you really change the experience on each of them? (00:28:40): I'll cover a couple with you. So let's do the risk one first. There's two risks we have. We have have FX risk, you come to Wise you see your rate, and then you may send us the money a little later. If you're moving a million dollars, you can't usually move it instantly. It might take you two to three days to move it. The rate's locked, could move against us, we'd lose some money. (00:29:01): So that cost, if you look back, so we've halved that cost over the last few years, and you can imagine through understanding the bits of the product, they generate exposure, and limiting it, and a bunch of algorithms behind that. But the more inspiring stuff is the people costs, and the partner costs, go through each of these one at a time. (00:29:25): So the people costs are our customer service team, operations teams. But I like to think of that as the cost of poor quality. So you bring up customer support if the products are clear, you hire lots of people in the back office. If you haven't automated it. We get like 20% improvement year on year as we're doing that. But come back to your question, how do you step change that? How do you do a 10x better experience? (00:29:49): I'll share with you a story from Singapore. It's quite a fun one. Because we went to Singapore about six, seven years ago, and [inaudible 00:29:58], we asked for a license. We had 20,000 people on the wait list, or so, saying, "Wise, please come to Singapore." And we went there, we asked the regular, "Hey, can you give us a license?" They gave us the license, but they said, "You have to physically meet every single customer."
turns.zh:
确实，市场体系越复杂，成本就越高。但先说说成本具体构成。看看我们的损益表，交易层面只有三项成本：人力成本、已实现风险成本，以及合作伙伴费用。（00:28:16）如果我们要实现“几乎零成本”转账的使命，就必须将现金流投入到技术研发中，以解决这三个难题。接下来，我简要说明每个难题的应对策略。记住，我们要比其他公司做得好十倍。那么如何彻底优化用户体验呢？（00:28:40）先讲风险控制。我们面临两种风险：外汇风险（用户在Wise平台看到汇率后，可能延迟汇款），以及交易延迟风险（百万美元级别汇款通常需要2-3天才能完成结算）。汇率锁定后，若汇率波动不利，我们就会遭受损失。

（00:29:01）过去几年，我们已将相关成本削减一半。通过产品设计优化（减少风险敞口）和算法优化，成本得以控制。但更值得关注的是人力成本和合作伙伴费用。先逐一分析。

（00:29:25）人力成本主要涉及客服团队和运营团队。但我更愿意将其视为低质量服务的成本——若产品设计清晰，后台流程自动化，这些团队的规模就能缩减。我们每年通过此类优化提升20%的效率。但回到核心问题：如何实现十倍级别的改进？（00:29:49）分享新加坡的案例。六七年前，我们申请当地牌照时，面对20,000名等待用户，监管部门要求所有客户必须亲自到场验证身份。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Face-to-face. And this happens, this is... Remember, they're banks that people use. So people go into banks usually, and you get face-to-face verified when you open a bank account. We're like, "You don't need to do this in Australia, in the UK, in other countries around the world." They're like, "In Singapore, for your license, you need to do this." So we actually sent a small team out to Singapore, and we opened an office through [inaudible 00:30:43], and customers... You went through this really slick flow, and then you got invited in to come see the team.
turns.zh: 面对面验证。这在新加坡是常规流程，因为当地银行普遍要求用户亲自到场开户。我们说：“在澳大利亚、英国等国家无需如此。”他们却坚持：“新加坡牌照必须执行此要求。”于是我们派小团队赴新加坡开设办事处，通过[00:30:43]的流畅流程，用户完成注册后即可与团队面谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太赞了。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: And customers hated it, and it was really expensive, obviously.
turns.zh: 当然，用户反感这种繁琐流程，成本显然也很高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: But the magic was we got the customers not to complain to us, but to complain to the government. And it took a year of lobbying, and a year of building, doing something unscalable effectively, before we got the world's first EKYC license in Singapore. So you could take a selfie, picture of your ID, and then you could get verified. (00:31:21): And that's what I call a 10x better experience than anyone else in the market, and that led to advocacy and word of mouth off the back of it. And that loop of getting your customers to help was also one of the learnings of word of mouth.
turns.zh: 但神奇的是，我们让客户不是向我们抱怨，而是向政府投诉。经过一年的游说和筹备，成功在新加坡获得了全球首张EKYC（电子身份验证）许可证。用户只需上传自拍照和身份证照片，就能完成验证。（00:31:21）这比市场上其他任何同类产品都要好十倍，由此引发了口碑传播和客户推荐。让客户帮助我们的这个循环，也是口碑传播的关键经验之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was the product team involved? Were you involved in that on the ground stuff? Or was it like [inaudible 00:31:40]?
turns.zh: 产品团队参与其中了吗？您亲自参与过这些实际工作吗？还是说（00:31:40）……？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Generally when we go [inaudible 00:31:43], we're running cross-functional teams, but this is a verification team. The team actually would verify the docs when you sent it to us. They went out to Singapore, verified them onsite, face-to-face. (00:31:54): So the fun bit here is why would customers help a company? And this is one of the other learnings on word of mouth. The way I think about this is that there are the rational reasons why people recommend, which we've covered. But there's these emotional ones as well. Softer ones people would call brand. I prefer to call it on the mission. (00:32:19): So we do our mission, which is to make the world's money move instantly at the touch of a button, for almost nothing. It was a very personal thing, it was like an internal company thing, to think our customers cared about it. And then we rebranded like eight, nine years ago, our first rebrand, and we wrote our mission and sent it to our customers. (00:32:41): We got more new customers from that email being forwarded around than any other kind of marketing. And I show this when I talk at conferences. This email broke all the rules of marketing. It didn't have a call to action, it didn't have a button to sign up, it didn't have anything in it, but people just forwarded it around saying, "You should check out Wise." (00:32:59): And it's not all the customer base, but there was a proportion of the customer base that this resonated in. And I think it's the authenticity within which they could see that we were genuinely trying to.... Trying to bring the prices down was a scheme to help us grow faster, which is kind of where it started out, was actually genuinely because founders, they were really upset about how much it cost to money. (00:33:27): They found good ways to solve that problem, and they're still really passionate about solving that problem. And they could see that authenticity flows through the whole company, because we got a... When you look at Wise, we're full of people on visas, and immigrants, and people that have worked, and live around the world, and struggled with this problem, and are passionate about solving it. And so they wanted to help us solve it. So the second part of this word of mouth engine is for us, we managed to get this mission thing to work. (00:33:53): So somehow we emotionally connect our cause, and then I see going, taking a step back, getting 10x better on price is through our customers helping us do it, which gets us even cheaper, which then brings more customers, that then creates this flywheel that's spins around.
turns.zh:
是的，是的。通常我们组建跨职能团队，但这次是验证团队。团队会亲自验证用户提交的文件。他们亲自前往新加坡，面对面核实证件。（00:31:54）有趣的是，客户为什么会帮助公司？这也是口碑传播的另一个启示。我认为人们推荐产品有理性原因，我们之前已经讨论过。但也有情感因素，比如品牌忠诚度。我更愿意将其归因于使命感。
（00:32:19）我们的使命是让全球资金一键即时流动。八九年前，我们首次重塑品牌，明确了使命并向客户传递。我们通过这封邮件获得了比其他任何营销活动都多的新用户。这封邮件打破了营销常规，没有行动呼吁，没有注册按钮，内容空白，但人们只需转发即可。（00:32:59）并非所有客户都被触动，但一定比例的客户产生了共鸣。这源于真实性，他们能感受到我们真心致力于降低转账成本。最初的初衷是帮助公司快速发展，但后来发现创始人对高昂转账费用的痛心才是根本动机。
（00:33:27）他们找到了解决方案，并始终充满热情。公司文化也渗透着这种真实精神——团队成员来自世界各地，曾深受跨境转账困扰，满怀热情致力于解决问题。因此他们愿意帮助我们。口碑引擎的第二环在于，我们成功让使命感落地。（00:33:53）通过情感共鸣，让客户参与降价行动，最终降低成本，吸引更多用户，形成良性循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a flywheel you guys have built. This reminds me of a lot of different things. One is you talked about how there's the reality of the things people need, and then there's this soft, fuzzy stuff that's harder to quantify. I actually is the framework just like that on that product I talked about of instant booking. (00:34:27): I kind of built a roadmap around the reality of what people actually need in order to feel comfortable, guests booking instantly. And then I call it the perception, what are their fears about letting guests book instantly? And there's a lot of work to just convince them, you think you're going to get all these guests that are really scary or whatever, but in reality it never happens. It's really rare something bad happens, and if it does, we're going to cover it. (00:34:50): So, I think that's a really cool framework when you're trying to get people to adopt something, is think about what do they actually need? And then how do you convince them of the things that are just in their head? And it sounds like the win there was kind of this sharing your mission and your values as a business.
turns.zh: 你们搭建的这个飞轮真是太棒了。这让我联想到很多事情。其中之一是，你们提到过现实中人们真正需要的东西，还有那些难以量化的模糊概念。我实际上在谈论的那款即时预订产品，其框架就是如此。（00:34:27）：我围绕人们实际需要的东西构建了一个路线图，让他们感到安心，比如客人可以即时预订。我把这部分称为"认知"——他们对即时预订持何种担忧？要说服他们并非易事。你可能以为会遇到很多可怕的客人，但实际上这种情况很少发生。即便有问题，我们也能妥善处理。（00:34:50）：所以，我认为当你试图让人们接受某种东西时，一个很棒的框架就是思考他们真正需要什么。然后再如何说服他们那些只存在于他们脑海中的担忧。这听起来很棒，关键在于分享你的使命和价值观。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, it just sounds, again very tweedy, right? Tweedy, like sounds very corporate, sounds like it's never going to work, but I think it's also... I mean, Airbnb, the authenticity is there. People are passionate about making that experience work for both sides of the marketplace. It's kind of clear. So, I'm kind of taking a step back, personally very passionate about customer-led growth, and how that turns into shareholder value. (00:35:32): So, taking a step back, where every business I've ever worked in, it's always got these two lists, a list of things to do for your customers, and then it's got a list of things to do to make money. And you generally do everything you need to do to make money, and you do two things with the customer list, and you go, "Customer led business." And then, neat thing about wise, and I'm pretty sure you'll see the same thing on Airbnb is, we just had one list, which is this list of things that you need to do to make customers happy, and it's prioritized by impact on the really hard things. And if you do these really hard things, they have an incredible impact for customers, but hence on your growth, and on your shareholder value.
turns.zh: 是啊，这听起来又很老生常谈，对吧？老生常谈，听起来很公司化，可能觉得这永远行不通，但我觉得……我是说Airbnb确实有真诚的一面。人们热衷于让这种体验对市场双方都奏效。这很明显。所以我个人退一步讲，我对以客户为导向的增长很感兴趣，以及它如何转化为股东价值。（00:35:32）：退一步说，我在之前工作的每个公司，都有两份清单，一份是为客户做的事，另一份是赚钱的手段。而赚钱的手段通常占据主导，客户清单上的事务只做两件事，然后就宣称"这是以客户为导向的业务"。而Wise的一个巧妙之处，我相信在Airbnb你也会发现同样的情况，就是我们只有一份清单，列出让客户满意的关键事项，并按对最难解决的问题的影响程度排序。如果你解决了这些难题，对客户、增长和股东价值都会产生巨大影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. Airbnb is not quite like that. It's actually become more like that with a lot of just like, "Let's build awesome products and not focus on experiments as much." So that's really interesting that prioritization basically at Wise came from, "What are people telling us?" I guess let me ask actually, how did you know what the impact would be on customers? How did you decide? Is it frequency of how often people request it? Is it, "We need to lower the cost, and so we're just going to prioritize the things that will lower prices most?"
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。Airbnb其实不完全是这样。实际上，随着公司发展，它变得越来越像Wise了。我们现在更倾向于"专注打造出色的产品，而不是过多尝试新项目"。所以很有意思的是，Wise的优先级排序基本上源于"人们告诉我们什么"。我想问一下，到底是如何判断这些措施对客户的影响的？你们是如何决定的？是根据人们请求的频率吗？还是"我们需要降低成本，所以优先处理能大幅降低价格的措施”？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Definitely on the journey at the beginning, you are into split testing, right? Let's try to take apart a split test on price. So, you've systemically dropped the cost. Imagine we drop the cost. The question is, do we drop the price? Do we pass that all on to customers? And do we keep some of it? And split testing on the price thing, if the split test is going to mean you end up with more revenue, it means you drop the price by 10%, and there happened to be that day, more than 10% more customers in the market who, they saw the price at one pound, but they see the price at 90p, at 10% lower, and they're like, "I wasn't going to shift at buy at one pound but I'm going to buy it 90p." (00:37:23): So this is pretty hard to do this. This word around conviction is one I use a lot, where you build this conviction that price is what matters. And through this incremental split test, you will take a long time to go there, but at some point you kind of go, "Actually I've got enough conviction." So there's one kind of strategic bet at the heart of Wise. That is if we have the lowest cost platform, and it's really fast, and really high quality, the world's volume will switch to us. And just marginally getting there step by step by step, and trying to track the incremental return is actually slower. And there's a point that comes that you go, "I feel really comfortable investing in price. I feel comfortable investing in speed, because I know it's going to pay back, and not necessarily this month, but eventually it will, and I need to make gains on all three levers in order to get there." Does that make sense?
turns.zh:
毫无疑问，在最初的探索阶段，你们肯定进行过分割测试，对吧？让我们来拆解一下价格方面的分割测试。假设你们系统性地降低了成本。想象一下，如果我们进一步降价，问题来了：是直接把降价幅度全部转嫁给客户，还是保留一部分利润？针对价格分割测试，如果最终能带来更多收入，那意味着你需要降价10%。但当天市场上恰好有超过10%的客户原本看到价格为1英镑，现在看到降价至90便士（即降价10%），他们会想：“我原本不打算买，但现在只要90便士，我肯定会入手。”（00:37:23）  
要做到这点其实很难。“建立价格至上的信念”是我常用的术语。通过逐步的分割测试，你可能需要很长时间才能达成共识，但最终你会说：“我对价格的信念足够坚定了。”  Wise的核心战略赌注是，如果我们拥有成本最低、速度最快、质量最高的平台，全球用户量就会向我们转移。但逐步推进这个过程，追踪边际回报其实很慢。直到某个时刻，你会说：“我对降价和提速的信心十足，因为我知道这些投入终将获得回报，或许不是本月，但最终必将实现。为了达成目标，我需要在三个维度上同时提升表现。” 这样理解对吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So essentially, in that track of work, instead of everything that you did to reduce price, there wasn't an experiment to see, "What impact does this have on growth, or revenue?" Instead, it's just, "We know reducing price is going to help us grow, and so we're just going to track how much we're cutting price." And that's essentially the goals, I imagine, were just cut the price by some amount, find a way to make it this much cheaper every, say, quarter, or year.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。换句话说，在那个阶段，你们没有通过实验来验证“降价对增长或收入有何影响”，而是直接基于信念行动：“我们知道降价能促进增长，所以就持续追踪降价幅度。”我猜当时的目标可能是：每季度或每年降低一定幅度的价格，逐步降低成本。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, that's it. You got it. And that conviction is core. That extends to our product management approach on the UX. So this is a great line for use internally, I'm sure you've heard it, "You can't split test your way to love." So, this experiment led product management approach, where you throw a bunch of things on the wall, and then you kind of see what sticks, and generally we don't advocate this. Obviously there's a bit of it that happens, but generally don't advocate it. Mainly because engineering is expensive, and you can actually figure out what matters to customers through other means. Some of the techniques we've talked, and build it. (00:39:21): There's a story I like to share. I had a product manager join our refer a friend team, viral growth team, and invite team, and after a quarter, I said, "So what are you going to build?" And he's like, "I'm going to test everything. I'm going to test the landing page, I'm going to test the subject line, I'm going to test the program so I don't know yet till run through all the tests, then I'm going to come back and tell you what I'm going to build." (00:39:47): I said, "You're not going to do this. I'm going to give you three weeks and you're going to pick one thing to change, but you're going to go talk to people, and get quantitative insights, and build your own gut feel around what matters, and then launch it, and submit, test it, and see if it works." But this thing of building conviction on what matters, and I watch how teams slowly build this and you need the data there to make sure it doesn't become a hubris, right? That enables you to make much bigger changes than just experimenting away, and it forces you to get clear on what actually is the problem to solve here, and how do I solve it really, really well? Does that make sense, Lenny, Do you disagree? It's a bit provocative there. Some people are pretty strong in the expert led approach.
turns.zh:
是的，就是这样。你们懂的。这种信念至关重要。这也延伸到我们在用户体验方面的产品管理策略。所以这句话在内部很常用，我相信你们也听过：“你无法通过分裂测试来赢得用户喜爱。” 所以，这种实验性产品管理方法——你把一堆东西抛向墙壁，然后看看哪些能站住脚——我们通常不提倡这种做法。显然这种情况偶有发生，但我们不主张这么做。主要是因为工程开发成本高昂，而你其实可以通过其他方式弄清楚对客户真正重要的东西。比如我们提到的某些技巧，再结合实际情况去落地。

（00:39:21）：我有个故事想分享。有位产品经理加入了我们的邀请用户团队、病毒式增长团队和推荐朋友团队。一个季度后，我问他：“你打算做什么？” 他回答：“我要测试所有东西。测试登陆页面，测试邮件标题，测试整个项目。直到所有测试完成后，我才能确定最终要做什么。” 

（00:39:47）：我说：“你不能这样做。我给你三周时间，你必须选定一个要改进的点。但你得去和用户交流，获取定量反馈，形成自己的直觉判断，然后上线、测试、观察效果。”但这种建立核心信念的过程很重要。我观察到团队是逐步建立这种信念的，而数据反馈能避免自满情绪。这能让你做出比单纯实验更重大的改变，还能迫使你清晰地认识到真正需要解决的问题，以及如何真正高效地解决它。Lenny，你明白吗？你有不同意见吗？这观点可能有点激进，有些人更倾向于专家主导的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, there's many ways to do it. There's no right way, and it's working. So I'm not going to argue.
