(00:42:00): So, what I'm hearing essentially, the experimentation culture at Wise is instead of just run, test everything that you're thinking about, throw out a bunch of ideas and see how they go, it's more, "Let's just decide we believe in this idea, and let's go bigger there, and run an experiment. Maybe not even." Is that roughly how you think about it?
turns.zh: 没错，方法有很多种。没有一种方法是绝对正确的，但只要能行得通就行。既然如此，我不想争论这个了。（00:40:35）：本期节目由艺术投资平台Masterworks赞助，一些普通投资者在该平台上已实现35%的净收益。没错，35%的净收益，还有其他16次退出案例，其中包括10%和17%的净收益。过去27年间，当代艺术的表现远超标普500指数，幅度达136%。花旗银行和德勤报告称，当代艺术作为抗通胀的避险资产表现出色，增值幅度与其他金融市场几乎无关。甚至贝莱德CEO拉里·芬克也称其是全球最重要的财富储备之一。不过，以往要实际投资当代艺术，动辄就得花上数百万美元。但现在Masterworks让几乎所有人都能投资班克西、巴斯奎特和莫奈等艺术家的作品。（00:41:22）：事实上，Masterworks上个月的最新退出案例，再次为投资者带来了两位数的年化净收益。自《纽约时报》2019年首次报道以来，他们已吸引超80万用户，部分新品在几分钟内就售罄。不过，您可以通过masterworks.art/lenny获得特别访问权限，跳过候补名单。与任何投资一样，过往表现不代表未来表现。投资涉及风险。重要法规及披露信息请参见masterworks.com/cv。再次强调，点击masterworks.art/lenny可直接跳过候补名单。（00:42:00）：所以，我理解的Wise的实验文化是，不是一味地去尝试，而是先确定我们相信这个想法，然后放手一搏，进行实验。甚至可能不做实验。您对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. And is that something that you've seen yourself in practice elsewhere?
turns.zh: 对，对，对，对。对，我在其他地方也见过类似的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how many parallels there are to Airbnb, because this is what Airbnb is doing now. There's been a shift recently, where instead of everything is very data experiment driven, it's very just like, "Let's build really great products that the founders are really excited about, and that the execs are hearing from people. Let's just build things that are awesome and launch them, and we believe things will grow." And Airbnb is doing great.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这与Airbnb有很多相似之处，因为Airbnb现在也在这样做。最近出现了转变，不再是数据驱动的实验，而是更倾向于“让我们打造真正令创始人兴奋、让高管从用户那里得到反馈的优质产品。让我们开发出令人惊叹的产品并推出它们，我们相信它们会发展壮大。”Airbnb现在做得很棒。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, the challenge of this is because it does become this risk thing of where it's like, okay, it's someone's opinion, so I think it's X, right? And everyone thinks they're kind of Steve Jobs type thing.
turns.zh: 是的，挑战在于这会变成一种冒险——比如，“好吧，这是某人的观点，所以我认为是X，对吧？” 每个人都觉得自己像史蒂夫·乔布斯那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That's right.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: You have some way of using data to get this conviction, and show why this is what we should do, but try to learn how to build that faster CME, slight difference. So, it's less product managers or me saying, "Hey guys, I think it's X." It's generally data driven, and qualitative insights driven as well.
turns.zh: 您有某种方法利用数据获得这种信念，并展示为什么我们应该这样做，但要学会如何更快地建立CME，略有不同。所以，不再是产品经理或我说“嘿，伙计们，我认为是X。” 现在通常是数据驱动的，也是定性洞察驱动的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Personally, I would always index towards running experiments just to put this out there, but I think in this case, it makes sense, where you just know, "We need to do these three things, just make it cheaper, make it faster." You don't need to AB test every idea there. Probably the main downside of not testing everything is you may be hurting things along the way, and you may not know it.
turns.zh: 就我个人而言，我总是倾向于优先进行实验——先说说我的看法。但我认为在这种情况下，按部就班做事也是合理的——你只需明确三个目标：降低成本、提高效率。没必要对每个想法都进行A/B测试。可能不测试所有方案的主要弊端在于，你可能会在过程中搞砸某些事情却浑然不觉。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: I mean, yeah, so we definitely do... So you're right. But there's a very different thing to when you look at the... From a sample size perspective, you want to do a beta, and understand the negative impact. It's a holdout group that's smaller, than a test to get a significance. It's quite define the criteria to know whether something is breaking, is generally a different thing to say, is this a material result in a test? Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。所以你说得对。但这和从样本量角度考虑beta测试有很大不同。beta测试需要更小的保留组来衡量负面影响，而测试显著性则需要更大的样本量。要判断某个功能是否崩溃，需要明确的标准，这和判断某个测试是否产生了实质性效果是两回事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And along those lines, the other benefit of experimentation is you know the impact. And so, team members can understand, "Here's what I did this quarter, this year." How do you think about just like performance reviews, and people's impact, and that kind of thing?
turns.zh: 说到这儿，实验的另一个好处是能清楚衡量影响。这样团队成员就能清楚：“这是我本季度、本年度完成的任务。”你如何看待绩效评估、个人的贡献之类的事情？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, that's a good one. This one is definitely an ongoing debate. So, I generally ask teams what's their impact? So, every quarter, every team, what... [inaudible 00:44:29] or Kristo will ask, "What did you ship?" And I generally ask, "How many people used it? What was the impact on volume?" Et cetera. And we have analyst teams that can answer this either with pre-post analysis, all kinds of techniques, or all through split tests. We generally have this, the debate is where the analysis slows us down, and we wouldn't make a decision off the back of the analysis. (00:44:54): And then, this generally is what you said, where the team needs a validation, mainly for themselves, and maybe a little performance, but not too much. And so, there were ways in which you can maybe get some read on it that isn't quite as strong as a split test, which we'd use in these things. It's more just getting some... You can understand that people worried when you do split tests that slow down the release of something, but in order to get impact, if you know you're not going to roll it back, then okay, you should just roll it out, and try to reduce the need for that validation.
turns.zh: 嗯，这确实是个长期争论的话题。所以我通常会问团队：你们的贡献是什么？每个季度，每个团队，都有什么成果？[00:44:29的语音模糊]或者Kristo会问：“你们推出了什么产品？”我通常会问：“有多少人使用了它？对业务量有什么影响？”等等。我们有分析团队，可以通过前后对比分析、各种技术手段或分组测试来解答这些问题。我们通常会遇到这样的情况：分析会拖慢决策进程，我们不会仅凭分析结果来做决定。（00:44:54）然后，这正如你所说，团队需要验证，主要是为自己验证，可能也需要一些绩效数据，但不必过多。因此，有一些方法可以了解情况，虽然不如分组测试那么有力，但我们也会用这些方法。人们担心分组测试会拖慢产品发布进度，但为了获取影响力，如果你知道不会回滚，那就应该直接上线，并尽量减少验证需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that there's an interesting correlation between products that grow through word of mouth, and less need to experiment with everything. Airbnb is also actually 70% of growth is word of mouth from the last stat that I heard. And then you think about all these social consumer apps, they mostly grow through people sharing with their friends, and a lot of them come from just the founder's intuition of what a great product's going to be. I think about Snapchat, and the recent mobile social apps. And so I think maybe there's something there about just as a founder, trusting your gut more often. But then it becomes difficult as you grow. You have to delegate, and then you have to trust people on your team making the right decisions. I guess, is there anything there that you've learned about just trusting individual product teams to make decisions that you can't for sure know are positive or negative without running experiments?
turns.zh: 我认为口口相传式增长的产品往往对全面实验的需求较低。就我听到的最新数据而言，Airbnb的增长中有70%来自口口相传。再看看那些社交消费类应用，它们大多通过用户分享实现增长，其中很多源于创始人对优秀产品的直觉判断。我想到Snapchat和近期的移动社交应用。所以我觉得或许作为创始人，更要相信自己的直觉。但随着公司发展，这变得越来越困难。你需要授权，然后信任团队成员做出正确决策。我想，你是否有过这样的经验：当你无法确定实验结果的正负面影响时，就放手让产品团队自行决策？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: So, as I say, almost everything we do, we have some way of understanding the impact. So, that's always there. We definitely have things where the team does something where Kristo or I will say, "This is just crazy. There's no way they're going to use this." And then we have a culture where people are encouraged to do these things, if they believe in it.
turns.zh: 正如我所说，我们所做的几乎每一件事，都能通过某种方式来评估其影响。因此，这种思维始终存在于我们的工作中。当然，确实有一些情况下，团队会提出某个想法，而克里斯托或我会说"这简直太疯狂了，用户绝不会用这个功能"。但在我们的文化中，只要团队成员坚信某个创意，就被鼓励去尝试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that?
turns.zh: 能举个例子吗？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, a couple. So the one [inaudible 00:46:52] that my head of SEO always talks about is a currency converter. So, the Wise homepage is a pretty good currency converter. It's got a decent one on there. There's tons of traffic on currency converter. So, if you click Wise link, now it's a little bit hidden on send, it's there. It's pretty cool. Currency converter.
turns.zh: 有几个例子。比如，SEO主管常提到的货币转换器功能。Wise的主页上就有一个不错的货币转换器，流量巨大。如果你点击Wise的链接，现在它被隐藏在发送按钮后面，但还是很方便使用。这功能很酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh I see it at the bottom there. Yeah, it's like [inaudible 00:47:13].
turns.zh: 哦，我在底部看到了。是啊，就像[00:46:52的模糊音频]一样。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: But if you Google currency converter, there's tons of traffic, and that converter on the Wise homepage obviously includes our price, and lets you sign up. And so, should we build a currency convertor? Should we try to capture this traffic? Is it more effective to try to push our own product there? And you can kind of understand why it was Kristo, actually not me, that was like, "This is a crazy idea." And the founder, and the SEO team went out and built it, and it's huge now, in terms of visits. I think we've got a currency convertor app out there. I think we've got [inaudible 00:47:51] out there, and yeah, people discover wise through that, as an example of off-topic traffic, but that's a good example of one of those things where yeah, the founder said, "No," or, "That's' a bad idea," and we kind of went ahead, and did it anyway.
turns.zh: 但如果你在谷歌上搜索货币转换器，流量巨大，Wise主页上的那个转换器显然包含了我们的价格信息，还能让用户注册。那么，我们是否应该开发一个货币转换器？是否要争取这些流量？在自己的产品中推广这个功能是否更有效？你可以理解为什么克里斯托（而不是我）会觉得这是个疯狂的想法。创始人和SEO团队最终开发了这个功能，现在它的访问量非常大。我记得我们还有一个货币转换器应用。人们通过这个功能发现Wise，这就是一个典型的非核心业务领域的成功案例，但这也说明了创始人有时会说“不行”或“这是个糟糕的主意”，然后团队还是坚持去做，最终取得了成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'm just thinking about broadly all the things we've been talking about. There's a couple of things that were floating around in my head. One is, reminds me of Amazon, where Jeff Bezos realized there are things that are going to be always true with Amazon. People always want cheaper prices, they want faster shipping. And I think there's something else. And it feels like you guys found the same sort of thing. What are the three things people always want with a money transfer product? And let's just make those as incredible as possible, and in your eyes, make them 10 times better than what anyone else has out there.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我正在思考我们讨论过的所有事情。其中有几个问题一直在我脑海中盘旋。一个让我想起亚马逊，杰夫·贝索斯意识到有些东西对亚马逊来说是永恒不变的。比如，人们总是希望价格更低，送货更快。我觉得还有其他因素。感觉你们也找到了类似的机会。那么，转账产品中，人们最常需要的三个功能是什么？让我们把这些功能做到极致，在你们眼中，比其他任何同类产品都要好十倍。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, totally. The business one example is relevant, and use it a lot when we talk to investors in the market, [inaudible 00:48:49] public helps validate this low cost, cutting price story. What's interesting is what changed though. So we started with transfers, but we got to account, and then we got to enterprise. Just what changed was we realized with account, if you just have to move $10, you're not going to download an app and do it. If you do it once, you're just going to do it in your bank. And so, that was a little bit of the insight behind building the Wise account, and we kind of focused on, there's a real problem with international banking. (00:49:22): So, really good example is for businesses. So if you are a business, say, in... Say a business in Europe, you've got a customer in Australia, and you want to get paid, you send them an invoice in Euros, and someday, some money's going to turn up in your account, you're like, "I don't know." They paid you an AUD, it got changed by three banks on the way through. You don't know what it is. What you'd love to do is invoice them in AUD, and get AUD in your bank account. You might even have people who need to pay in AUD, so you have to call to keep it there. But to get an Australian bank account, I found out, you need to fly to Australia, you need to incorporate a business in Australia, you need to go to a bank with all those papers, and then they will give you an Australian bank account number.
turns.zh:
是的，完全正确。商业案例很贴切，我们在向市场上的投资者介绍产品时经常用到这个例子[00:48:49]。公众对低成本、降价策略的认可度很高。但有趣的是，市场环境发生了变化。我们最初从转账业务起步，后来拓展到账户服务，再到企业客户业务。关键在于我们意识到，用户如果只需转账10美元，是不会下载应用来操作的。如果转账一次，他们很可能直接通过银行完成。因此，构建Wise账户的核心洞察在于，跨境银行服务存在严重痛点。

（00:49:22）：企业客户的需求也很典型。比如欧洲企业向澳大利亚客户开具欧元发票后，收款方汇入澳元时，款项要经过三家银行转换，汇率波动让企业无从知晓。理想的解决方案是直接开设澳元账户，方便收款和提现。有些企业甚至需要强制客户使用澳元支付，导致客户不得不打电话沟通操作流程。但实际上，要在澳大利亚开设账户，需要亲自飞往澳大利亚注册公司，再携带所有文件到银行开户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: So with Wise, you can get an Australian bank account number with three clicks. Anyone can, and any business can, and you get an Australian balance, and a US, and a UK, and a Swiss bank. And this is killer for businesses that receive money internationally. And then the next big jump we did, and for consumers, so there are plenty of people, if all your banking is in the US, you probably shouldn't use Wise, but if you're somebody who uses another currency a lot, then you probably should use us as your primary bank. (00:50:37): There's some people, for example, who live in one country and get paid in another currency, and this is... Wise is great as an account for managing that. And we found with that, we got about... As we launched the account in markets, it was about a 20 to 30% more volume, cross-border volume coming into Wise from that market. Just a good example of how, while it's not price, not speed, you could argue is kind of ease of use, but we had to evolve it in order to get to the next tranche of the market. Does that make sense, Lenny?
turns.zh:
通过Wise，三步即可开设澳大利亚账户。任何企业都能轻松实现跨境收款。例如，用户若常用其他货币，完全可以将我们作为主账户使用。
（00:50:37）：有些跨境收款群体尤其受益，比如生活在某国却用别国货币收款的用户，Wise账户能完美管理资金流转。数据显示，开通澳元账户后，相关市场的跨境转账量增长了20%至30%。这充分说明，尽管价格和速度不是核心竞争力，用户体验才是关键。为了拓展市场，我们必须不断优化产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. And it all just comes back from what would be the theoretical ideal situation for people transferring money, say from Australia. And what I'm hearing is just find all the little friction points that get in the way. In this case you're like, "Okay, we'll create you an Australian bank account, and you don't even worry about it."
turns.zh: 完全正确。归根结底，Wise要解决的是跨境转账的痛点。比如为澳大利亚用户开设账户，省去繁琐的注册流程，让资金管理更便捷。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, that's exactly it. And so now then you have all these other problems, because we've got about $12.5 billion in deposits now, which is like a time. And the next problem customers are at is, "I want a return." And we quite deliberately don't have a banking license. You have to figure out, how are we going to solve that? We now put customers money in government bonds, US bonds, and when you pay with your card, it dynamically sells those bonds. And that's how we give you an interest rate, in roundabout 5% right now, given where bond rates are.
turns.zh: 是的，就是这样。现在我们遇到了其他一系列问题，因为我们现在有大约125亿美元的存款，这是一个巨大的挑战。客户目前面临的下一个问题是：“我想要回报。” 而我们故意没有银行牌照。你得想办法怎么解决这个问题？现在我们把客户的钱投资于政府债券和美国国债，当你用卡支付时，系统会动态出售这些债券。这就是我们目前能提供大约5%利率的原因——毕竟债券利率就这么高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, interest rates are quite high, for better or worse. Zooming out a little bit, for folks that are starting to... Their wheels are turning, they're like, "Okay, I want to think about word of mouth, driving word of mouth. I'm going to go look at my survey results. I'm going to figure out these pillars that are driving word of mouth. I'm going to think about how to make things 10 times better." Just broadly, for someone that's starting to approach this, what would you say to them? How should they approach this? Any major learnings at a higher level, of just how to drive word of mouth for a product?
turns.zh: 是的，利率确实很高，不管是好是坏。再宏观一点，对于那些刚开始... 他们脑子里的齿轮开始转动，他们会想：“好吧，我要考虑口碑，推动口碑。我要去看看我的调查结果。我要找出推动口碑的支柱。我要想怎么把事情做得好十倍。” 对于刚开始接触这个的人，你会怎么说？他们应该怎么做？在更高层面上，关于如何推动产品口碑，有什么主要的经验教训吗？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: I think it just comes back to talking to customers and this is the question we've kept coming back to. What would it take to make it 10x better? And then you get clear in your head what it would take, and then it's usually the thing that everyone's looked at before and thought, it's the thing that's impossible. One more example is on the partner side. So, rather than find a cheaper bank for a banking partner, you think, well, the cheapest banking partner is the central bank. And imagine you're a startup. How the hell do you get a bank account at the central bank? (00:53:08): But that kind of thinking, and we now have a bank account at the Bank of England, the National Bank of Singapore, Bank of Australia. And each of these was as hard as getting that face-to-face verification thing in Singapore. It took years of lobbying, and all kinds of stuff, in order to make it happen. But it's setting your goal all the way up there. That's what enables you to build a 10x better product. That's what gets you to the word of mouth. So, the first step is getting super clear on what's the problems that my customers are caring about, worrying about? And then once you're clear there, as you said, how can I solve that completely, and what's the best it could possibly be? And then the hard bit is figuring out how to move that.
turns.zh: 我认为这归根结底就是与客户对话，这是我们不断探讨的问题。怎样才能让产品好十倍？然后你会清楚需要做什么，而通常这些事情别人之前都想过，但认为不可能。比如在合作伙伴方面。与其找一个更便宜的银行合作伙伴，你会想，最便宜的银行合作伙伴是中央银行。想象一下你是一家初创公司。怎么可能在中央银行开一个账户呢？（00:53:08）但这种思维方式，我们现在在英格兰银行、新加坡国家银行、澳大利亚银行都开设了账户。每一步都像在新加坡获取面对面验证一样困难。花了多年游说，各种努力，才最终实现。但就是要把目标定得足够高。这才让你能打造出好十倍的产品。这才让你能获得口碑。所以第一步是清楚客户关心、担心的哪些问题。然后一旦你清楚了这些，你就可以说，如何彻底解决这些问题？怎样才能做到最好？然后最难的部分就是想办法实现它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of these things you're talking about are just, they sound like they are either impossible, like no way we're going to achieve that, or really, really hard. And a lot of companies, and a lot of founders, teams are just like, "Okay, we're not ever going to create a bank here. We're not going to be able to create an Australian bank account for everyone." What is it about your culture, or approach to these problems that you think that's unique to Wise that's like, "No, we're going to spend three years figuring this out, because it's that important?"
turns.zh: 你提到的很多事情听起来要么是不可能的，比如我们绝对做不到，要么就是非常困难。很多公司和创始人、团队都会想：“好吧，我们永远不会在这里创办一家银行。我们没法为每个人都开设澳大利亚银行账户。” 你们的文化或处理这些问题的方法有什么独特之处，让你们觉得“不，我们要花三年时间解决这个问题，因为这太重要了”？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: I think it's two [inaudible 00:54:17]. So one is, definitely the founders have this philosophy that unless you're doing something hard and new, it's kind of a waste of time. So, I think that also kind of runs through the culture. So, it's quite a rude awakening when people join Wise, because they're like, "Okay, I'm going to come, and just play around with a few things." You're like, "No, actually, the culture of the product team is we're super incentivized to do the hard things, and that's what's rewarded." (00:54:46): And that's quite hard to create the air cover. You can imagine like then in the early days and months when growth was slow, and people turned on the money taps in marketing, and you're trying to keep focused and plugging your away up these hard things, it's quite hard also to get the management cover in order to let the teams keep doing this. And then it's also hard just to turn up to work and really keep... You can imagine being in Singapore, verifying customers face-to face, thinking, "This is going nowhere, this is going nowhere, this is going nowhere." And then suddenly it changes. So that's what progress very much feels like at Wise. And we try to recognize that, and create a culture that enables that.
turns.zh: 我觉得有两个原因（00:54:17，声音不清晰）。首先，创始人秉持这样一种理念：除非你在做一些高难度、创新性的工作，否则做任何事都只是在浪费时间。这也深深渗透在公司的文化之中。因此，当新员工加入Wise时，他们往往会感到震惊——“好吧，我来这儿就是想随便尝试点新东西。”而你会说：“不，实际上产品团队的文化是，我们极其鼓励挑战难题，努力攻克难关才会获得回报。”（00:54:46）要营造这种文化氛围实属不易。想象一下，初创期和早期阶段，增长缓慢，市场部门疯狂砸钱做营销，而你却要专注于解决难题，保持团队专注力，这时要获得管理层的支持以让团队持续推进工作也绝非易事。再比如，在新加坡实地验证客户时，面对面交流却毫无进展，你会不断质疑“这条路走不通，这条路走不通，这条路走不通。”但最终情况会峰回路转。这正是Wise的进展之道。我们努力认清这一点，营造有助于推动进展的文化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like there's also just a lot of patience for these things. There isn't like, "We need to hit this quarterly goal. Why aren't we creating banks in Singapore yet?"
turns.zh: 这里似乎对这些事情有着极大的耐心，没有那种“我们必须达成季度目标，为什么我们还没在新加坡开设银行分行？”的紧迫感。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. The other kind of metaphor that's rolling around my head is something Seth Godin talks about. I don't know if you've heard of this guy, he's a marketing guru, and he has this concept that you want to build something that's remarkable, because if something is remarkable, it'll spread. And if you think about the word remarkable, it's something worth remarking about, which essentially is word of mouth.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我脑海中一直盘旋着赛斯·高汀提到的另一种比喻。不知道你是否听说过他，他是营销大师，提倡打造引人注目的事物，因为引人注目的事物会自发传播。回想“引人注目”这个词，本质上就是口口相传。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so that's his kind of mission and his, I don't know, advice to people is build something remarkable, something people will want to remark about. And clearly, you all have been doing that. And that's actually a good segue to where I wanted to go, which is around how you structure your team, and how you incentivize the team, organize teams, to achieve all these sorts of things. So, maybe just broadly, is there something unique to how you think about work structure, incentives, goals, things like that, in order to achieve these really hard things?
turns.zh: 所以这就是他的使命和建议——打造引人注目、值得人们津津乐道的事物。显然，你们一直在践行这一理念。这也正是我想探讨的核心问题——如何构建团队架构，如何激励团队，组织团队以达成这些高难度目标。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: There's two unique lenses on this. One is in the macro-structure and one is in the micro-structure. So at the macro level, if you look at actually international banks, they don't really exist. I'm not sure if you've moved around between countries, but say you open a bank account with Citibank in the US, and then you go to Citibank in the UK, your Citibank account doesn't exist in the UK. You have to go to Citibank in the UK, and open a Citibank account. And actually, turns out, with some of these banks, to move money between your bank accounts is an international transfer. It's crazy. (00:56:53): So, when you take a step back, and look at how the market looks, you have at one end, international banks which are local tech stacks. So there's a core banking system in the US, and one in the UK, and one in Europe, say for Citibank, or for HSBC, but they have deep local integrations, so they're directly integrated in the payment system. Citibank in the US has got relationships, say, with the Federal Reserve, et cetera. (00:57:20): Other end of the spectrum you've got something like PayPal. So it's a tech company, it's got a single global tech stack. It doesn't run a additional version of PayPal in Australia than to the US, but it doesn't have deep connections. It hasn't got five central bank accounts, it hasn't got any of that. And I'd like to think of in the middle, you've got Wise, where we have a single global tech stack, and we have deep local infrastructure. (00:57:45): Now, from a technological perspective, just take a step back and think through this. This is actually non-trivial to figure out how to design. So, let's take something like the onboarding flow. So, we have global product teams, one part of product teams called global product teams. So we have a single onboarding flow that will give you a Wise account, and it's the same code that runs, whether you are in Brazil, New York, or Australia. (00:58:17): The regulation in Australia and Brazil is really different, and it isn't black and white in any country. So, there's a bunch of... You get a bunch of things you just shouldn't do in terms of letting people get so [inaudible 00:58:31] people who shouldn't get access to accounts. And then you can need to check these people aren't using it, and different jurisdictions have completely different requirements. Example is Japan, you have to take a picture of that front of the ID, the back of the ID, and the side of your ID. It's the only country in the world that you have to do this.
turns.zh: 这一点有两个独特的视角。一个是宏观层面的，另一个是微观层面的。所以从宏观层面来看，如果你观察国际银行，它们实际上并不存在。我不确定你是否曾在不同国家之间迁移过，但比如说，你在美国花旗银行开设账户后，再去英国的花旗银行开户，英国的账户在美国是无法使用的。你必须去英国的花旗银行重新开户。事实上，一些银行在不同国家的账户转账会被视为跨境转账，这真是太疯狂了。（00:56:53）所以，当你退后一步审视市场时，可以看到一端是拥有本地技术栈的国际银行。比如花旗银行在美国、英国和欧洲都有核心银行系统，但它们与本地支付系统深度整合，比如美国的花旗银行与美联储等机构有合作关系。（00:57:20）另一端则是像PayPal这样的科技公司。它采用单一的全球技术栈，但在澳大利亚和美国的PayPal版本并不相同，而且缺乏深度本地化连接，比如它没有五个中央银行账户等。我认为中间还有像Wise这样的公司，我们拥有单一的全球技术栈，同时在本地也有深厚的基础设施。（00:57:45）从技术角度来看，要设计出这样的架构并非易事。以开户流程为例，我们有全球产品团队，部分产品团队成员被称为全球产品团队。因此，我们有统一的开户流程，无论你在巴西、纽约还是澳大利亚，都能获得相同的Wise账户，运行的代码也完全一致。（00:58:17）但澳大利亚和巴西的监管法规差异巨大，且各国监管标准并非非黑即白。比如，防止未经授权访问账户的措施在不同司法管辖区要求迥异。日本就要求用户上传身份证正面、背面及侧面照片，这是全球唯一强制执行此类要求的国家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: And imagine you're the product manager for onboarding, and someone tells you, "Design the onboarding flow to give somebody a bank..." Just imagine gathering all the requirements from every country in the world, because there's very little similarity. You can't just say, "I take the US," and copy it somewhere else. It's very, very, very different. (00:59:05): It'd take forever to try to get that, and then normalize that into the main model, and try to figure out how you're going to structure the data around this. So, it then becomes like, what is the organization structure that enables us to discover what the domain model, let's call it that, for the onboarding flow should look like. And you end up with a global product team that owns overall KPIs around conversion rate, et cetera. And you have local, regional teams that own the conversion rate, and the cost to do KYC for their market, and they contribute to the global product code base. (00:59:44): So we have weak product ownership, where anyone can make code change, and pull requests, and these guys owning the vision in the center. But the only way that vision can evolve is by getting the feedback from these guys in the market, as they're constantly pushing stuff forward. And through that process, artifacts start emerging, where other markets are like Japan, and so you start splitting off that, and creating subtypes for it, and slowly the model emerges from there. (01:00:09): And so with this structure, the thing to optimize for is a really hard one. That problem that every global business has, is how do you get this collaboration to work between the local and the global? But unlike every other business, most businesses solve this probably as you know, is you usually have the US, and then you have international. And international is usually a bump site, where everyone's arguing to get their thing prioritized, right?
turns.zh: 想象一下，你是负责新用户引导流程的产品经理，有人对你说：“设计新用户引导流程，让用户能在银行完成……” 试想一下，要收集全球各国的所有需求，因为各国差异极大。你不能简单地说“就用美国的方案”然后照搬到其他地方。这差别实在太大了。（00:59:05）：要收集这些需求再整合到主模型中，然后想办法构建数据结构，这得花费大量时间。因此，关键问题在于：如何构建一个组织架构，让我们能明确新用户引导流程的域模型（暂且这么称呼）。最终，我们组建了一个全球产品团队，负责整体转化率等关键指标，而本地团队则专注于各自市场的转化率和KYC成本，并为全球产品代码库贡献代码。（00:59:44）：所以我们的产品管理权责分工很模糊，任何人都能提交代码更改和拉取请求，而核心团队负责整体愿景。但愿景的演进必须依赖市场团队的反馈，因为他们在不断推进项目。通过这个过程，逐渐涌现出一些成果，比如日本市场的需求，于是我们开始为其拆分子类型，逐步形成成熟的模型。（01:00:09）：在这种架构下，优化目标变得异常艰巨。这是所有全球化企业的共同挑战——如何让本地团队与全球团队协同合作？但与其他企业不同的是，大多数企业可能采取“美国优先，国际市场其次”的策略。而国际市场通常是临时补丁区，各个团队都在争抢优先级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Whereas here, you're kind of letting the local teams commit directly to the code base, and then this global team's got this challenge of doing this, and we over time create sub-teams around parts of the regionalization of the structure, around different objects as they emerge. But that broadly speaking is the first problem, the global problem. And the other bit with us is this is quite unique to us, because most fintechs out there are usually in one market. Like you take Robin Hood, it was in the US, it came to the UK, they went back to the US. You take Monzo, only the UK, N26 only in Europe, Up in Australia, China, and the US. And that's because their home markets are so big, and one regulator is a ton of work to manage. And the second complexity we have is we have all of these markets we have to be in, because we're international by default. So a lot of our thinking is where do we take that, turn that into competitive advantage, and which customer base really needs that? Which is what zooms us into that positioning on the international account.
turns.zh: 而我们的做法是让本地团队直接向代码库提交代码，随后全球团队面临挑战，需要围绕区域化结构的不同部分创建子团队。这些子团队会随着新需求涌现而逐步形成。但总体而言，这是首要的全球化难题。另一个挑战则更为独特，因为多数金融科技公司只专注于单一市场。比如Robin Hood起步于美国，后来扩展至英国，又回归美国；Monzo仅服务英国；N26只在欧洲；Up则聚焦澳大利亚、中国和美国。这是因为他们的本土市场规模庞大，且单一监管机构就需要耗费巨大精力。更复杂的是，我们必须覆盖全球所有市场，因为我们默认就是国际化企业。因此，我们的核心思考在于如何将这一优势转化为竞争力，以及哪个客户群体真正需要这些功能。这正是我们在国际账户定位上的核心考量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It just comes back to again, and again, again and again, doing the hard thing, knocking peoples' socks off, and it feels like that's the formula for Wise.
turns.zh: 归根结底，还是要一次又一次地挑战极限，创造惊喜，这正是Wise的成功秘诀。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: I think yeah, you more or less got it. So that's one bit on structure. So this global local thing, and the second one has been a bit more of a journey. So when we started early on, we ran in autonomous independent teams, all focused on KPIs, and these KPIs rolled up to make it cheaper, make it faster, make it easier to use. You can imagine like a KPI tree, and teams around bits of their KPIs, and every quarter they talk through how they move their KPI, et cetera, and this kind of worked. And the way we ran our planning is, every quarter every team would stand up and talk through its plan, get feedback from other teams, and then move on. This worked till we got to 30 teams, and then you go from doing this in the afternoon, to doing it in two days and it's just like whoa. (01:02:27): So, we started heading towards the Spotify model, where we group the teams in squads, and into tribes. Today, I think that autonomy is at the squad level. So the squads are around products. So, we'll have a Wise account squad, a business squad, a Wise platform, our enterprise product squad, you'll have a North Am squad that looks after the North American product, and Lat Am squad, et cetera. And then financial crime fighting, et cetera. (01:02:57): And inside those squads you've got the teams, and the squad... Imagine you're the director for the Wise account, but you don't have a vision for the account. You've got to say where it's going. You've got to keep your teams on track against it. The teams aren't off doing whatever they want. They kind of need to be on track, versus the overall vision, and you're accountable for the results of that squad. And squads are in tribes, the tribe provides overall leadership, and a slight, light touch strategy on the squads. And that's more or less our structure, and how we've evolved towards it.
turns.zh: 我觉得是的，你基本理解得没错。先说结构部分。关于全球与本地化的关系，这个问题确实花了我们不少心思。最初我们采用的是自主独立的团队模式，所有团队都专注于关键绩效指标（KPI），通过汇总这些KPI来降低成本、提升效率、优化用户体验。你可以想象成一棵KPI树，每个团队围绕自己的KPI展开工作，每个季度汇报进展。这套模式在早期确实有效。但当团队扩展到30个时，原本下午开会汇报的流程，变成了两天密集讨论，效率直线下降。（01:02:27）于是我们开始借鉴Spotify的模式，将团队划分成小队和部落。如今，权力下放主要在小队层面——即围绕产品构建团队。比如Wise账户小队、商业小队、Wise平台、企业产品小队，还有专注北美和拉美市场的团队，以及金融犯罪打击小组等。（01:02:57）每个小队下设多个团队。以Wise账户小队为例，团队负责人需明确产品愿景，引导团队围绕目标推进工作。团队不能随心所欲，而是要与整体愿景保持一致，负责人要对小队的成果负责。小队隶属于部落，部落为小队提供战略指导和轻度管理。这就是我们逐步演进的组织架构。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else along the word of mouth concept that you think would be useful for people to share? Either how you think about it, team structure, anything else?
turns.zh: 在口碑传播方面，您认为还有哪些经验值得分享？无论是团队结构的思考，还是其他方面的经验？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: There's one tiny bit I'll share, which was around marketing and referral. This was super interesting for me. So, we've been running it, like Airbnb, we've been running referral program for now 12 years, and after 12 years, you've kind of tested everything anyway. And like I said, by this point you have literally tested everything. So when somebody comes up with something that has a 300% increase, you're like, "Whoa, that's super interesting. What just happened?"
turns.zh: 我再分享一个小例子，关于营销和推荐机制。这对我来说非常有启发。我们推行推荐计划已经12年，经过12年的实践，基本把所有可能性都测试过了。到这个阶段，你真的什么都试过了。所以当有人提出能带来300%增长的方案时，你会惊呼：“哇，太不可思议了。这是怎么做到的？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I'm excited for this.
turns.zh: 哇，我对这个很感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: And yeah, I'll share this one, because it's interesting. So we run many variants of refer a friend, where you'll get different kinds of benefit. We tried chocolate, we tried money, we've tried $200, $500, $10, you get some, I get some money, all kinds of things. More or less headed towards three for $100, generally it's a sweet spot. Anyway, it's a pretty creative PM there. And he was again talking to customers, and he spotted this thing, which is pretty cool, which is when you do a transfer with Wise, at the end you get this email, the email says, "Well done." Then it says, "Your money's there in the other person's account, and you saved $10 on this transfer." And he got this insight, which was pretty awesome, was he realized that people believed they saved money, but they didn't believe the number. And he then thought, what would it take to get them to believe the number?
turns.zh: 是啊，我会分享这个案例，因为它挺有趣的。我们推出了多种“推荐朋友”活动，每种活动都会带来不同形式的奖励。我们尝试过巧克力奖励、现金奖励，金额从200美元到500美元不等，用户分得一部分，我也分得一部分奖金，各种各样的形式。但最终发现，把金额定为100美元左右效果最佳，总体来说这个数字比较合适。总之，这是个相当有创意的市场营销策略。他再次与客户沟通时，发现了一个很酷的点：当用户通过Wise进行转账时，最后会收到一封邮件，邮件里写着“干得好”，接着会告知“你的钱已存入对方账户，本次转账节省了10美元”。他由此获得了一个深刻洞察——用户虽然觉得自己省了钱，但对具体金额却存在疑虑。于是他思考：怎样才能让用户相信这个数字呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That seems right.
turns.zh: 这样想挺对的。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: And so the fun bit was the approach. So then him and a designer sat there and they sketched out an alternative email, and they went down to the coffee shop downstairs, and they showed it to people, and they said... Just asked them what they thought, and they kept iterating it until they got to a graph. And this graph is like this... When you go through a money transfer thing, it pops up in places, behind the compare button. And this graph shows with your bank, when you send, how much is in the rate hidden as... This is how much you're sending, this is how much they're taking in the rate in a fee, and this is how much you can see in the fee, because the fees are hidden in the rates with banks. And then this is with Wise. (01:05:45): And they iterate this graph to the point that people looked at like, "Oh my God, I'm never using my bank again. This number... This is crazy." And then they put this graph on the success page when you did a transfer. Saying, "You saved this." And put a share button in there, and invite your friends button, and that's what really drove it. And when you fast-forward to today, we've now got... So it's actually quite hard. So, we now have I think about 70 bank accounts around the world. So, I think the top three accounts, banks in the world, where we log onto every day, and then we log the price and the quote for a bunch of different routes into a file. You can imagine how hard is. I think I personally have about 17 of these still in my name, that I've opened up around the world to help the team get going. But that's kind of one of the biggest word of mouth growth, or referral insights. I've got to this comparison thing, made into our marketing, made into our homepage, just went everywhere up from that insight.
turns.zh: 有趣的部分在于策略的创新。于是他和一位设计师一起构思替代方案，带着设计稿去楼下咖啡店展示，询问用户意见，不断优化，最终形成了一个图表。当用户进行转账时，图表会出现在不同位置，比如比较按钮后方。图表清晰展示了用户通过Wise转账时的汇率对比，银行端的汇率隐藏在费率中，用户只能看到实际支付的费用。而Wise的汇率则完全透明。（01:05:45）：他们不断优化图表设计，直到用户惊呼“天哪，我再也不用银行了！这个数字太不可思议了”。最终将图表置于转账成功页面，附上分享按钮和邀请好友功能，这才真正推动了用户增长。如今，我们已开通全球约70个银行账户，其中三大主流银行账户是我们日常登录使用的，并将不同路线的汇率和报价数据录入文件。可以想象这项工作的难度之大。我个人名下仍有17个全球开设的银行账户，帮助团队快速起步。这就是口碑传播和推荐机制的典范案例。通过将对比功能融入营销文案和主页设计，我们成功实现了病毒式传播。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you said that that like 3x'd the sharing rate?
turns.zh: 你说这个策略让分享率提升了三倍？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, that 3x'd the sharing rate. So we always had the share button after you completed a transfer. But putting that there with this graph, and that kind of got me to this, I'm curious on your take on this, on this definition of product marketing, where customers use the product, and they think they got this value, but when they actually know the value they get. So we got this on speed as well, where we're doing instant transfers, and customers wouldn't know it was instant. (01:07:21): So when you get an instant transfer, there's like this wizzy animation at the end, and you kind of know the money's in the other person's account, ready to spend. And again, you see this big jump in referral rate when that happens, but people need to know it's happened. And closing this delta between what you've done, and what's perceived to be done is what I call product marketing within the product. And that in its own right is a discipline, I've learned.
turns.zh: 是啊，这让分享率提高了三倍。所以我们总是在完成转账后才放置分享按钮。但把这个按钮放在图表旁边，这让我意识到，产品营销的定义是客户使用产品后认为获得了某种价值，但实际上他们并不知道自己获得了什么价值。我们在速度方面也做了改进，实现了即时转账，但客户并不知道这是即时的。（01:07:21）：当你收到即时转账时，最后会有一个炫酷的动画效果，你能感觉到钱已经到对方账户，可以随时消费了。再次强调，当这种情况发生时，推荐率会大幅提升，但用户需要知道这已经完成了。缩小你实际做出的和用户感知到的差距，这就是我所说的产品内产品营销。这种方法本身就是一门学科，我对此深有体会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome insight. It comes back to this framework we talked about of reality and perception, in a flip way, instead of getting people to adopt something, it's to appreciate the work you've done to make it remarkable, to make them understand how remarkable it really is.
turns.zh: 这真是深刻的见解。这回到了我们之前讨论的现实与感知的框架，不过是反向操作。不是让人们接受某样东西，而是让他们感激你为使产品卓越所做的努力，让他们明白产品有多出色。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, that was it. And that's something I'm continuously learning about yeah, as we go, as well.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。随着我们的推进，我也在不断学习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is extremely interesting. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, I know you also do a bunch of charity work, and I wanted to give you a chance to share what you're doing there.
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。在我们即将进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，我知道你还参与了很多慈善活动，我想借此机会分享一下你在慈善领域的经历。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny. So, less charity, essentially came out of angel investing, is probably the way to say it. So I invest in startups, generally fintechs, mission led founders, word of mouth type stuff, all the stuff we've been talking about, that I'm passionate about. It is less investing, more helping, and yeah, just getting through the angel route. And then over time, I realized the thing I'm most passionate about is market failures. So generally I find that the invisible hand means most human needs get fulfilled by the market, but there are a few things that don't, and there's a couple of exciting startups out there who work really hard in this space. A couple are Beam in the UK, working on homelessness, Affinity and Neobank in Ghana. And so, this type of thing is stuff I'm most passionate about. So, if any of your listeners out there know anyone doing anything of that kind, trying to solve these kinds of hard problems, definitely reach out, always keen to talk.
turns.zh: 谢谢，Lenny。说实话，我参与的慈善活动更多源于天使投资。基本上，我投资初创公司，特别是金融科技公司，关注使命驱动的创始人，口碑传播之类的，都是我们今天谈论过的、我热衷的领域。与其说是投资，不如说是提供帮助，通过天使投资的途径。随着时间推移，我意识到自己最热衷的是市场失灵问题。总的来说，我发现看不见的手意味着大多数人类需求能通过市场得到满足，但仍有一些需求无法被满足。有几家令人兴奋的初创公司在这方面做得很出色。比如英国的Beam，致力于解决无家可归问题，还有加纳的Affinity和Neobank。这些领域正是我的热情所在。所以，如果听众中有谁知道在解决这类难题的初创公司，欢迎联系我，随时愿意交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And we'll link to those two you mentioned in the show notes just in case people want to check them out. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会在节目笔记中附上你提到的这两家公司的链接，以便听众方便查看。接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.en: Let's go for it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 来吧。你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Two, one's at the other ends of the spectrum. So one is... This sounds terribly pretentious Crime and Punishment, and the other one is Midnight's Children by Salman Rushdie. I read a lot, I'm very passionate about reading, fiction, mainly. I don't read... Nonfiction is too much like work. And so, I generally need to read before I go to bed to decompress my brain. It's generally escapist type stuff. But I'm curious what you think of this, but for me authors are people that create people with words. (01:10:03): Like you say artist is a good artists if it's... Makes a good likeness to somebody, but imagine that you create somebody with words, and that person feels real, so they have some insight into the human condition. And what's amazing is if you learn something about what it means to be human from reading that. So at that end of the scale, Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment, where this guy kills somebody, and it just eats him up. It's a pretty amazing book. It's not as heavy as it sounds, but books like that are pretty awesome. So, I recommend that a lot. (01:10:37): And the other end of the scale is sometimes you read a book and there's a single sentence where each word has been just stitched together, and it's like, again, a work of art, and there, Rushdie is probably the pinnacle for me, of Midnight's Children, which is about partition in India, which is pretty... Through a metaphor, it's pretty amazing.
turns.zh: 嗯，两个极端。一个是……这听起来很装模作样——《罪与罚》，还有萨尔曼·拉什迪的《午夜之子》。我读了很多书，对小说特别感兴趣。我不怎么读非小说类书籍——非小说类书籍太像工作了。所以我通常睡前读点轻松的书。但我很好奇你怎么看待这个问题。对我来说，作家就是用文字创造人物的人。（01:10:03）比如你说艺术家，如果画得像某个人，那不错。但想象用文字创造出一个人，让人感觉很真实，那他对人类处境就有深刻洞察力。最棒的是，从阅读中能领悟到什么是做人的意义。在这个极端，陀思妥耶夫斯基的《罪与罚》，里面有个人杀了人，结果被内疚吞噬。这本书很棒，不像听起来那么沉重，但这样的书太棒了。所以我经常推荐它。（01:10:37）另一个极端，有时读到一本书，每个字都是拼凑起来的，但又像艺术品。对我来说，拉什迪的《午夜之子》是巅峰之作，讲印度分治问题，通过隐喻呈现得非常精彩。

turns.en: It's a beautiful answer. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 这回答得真棒。你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Oh gosh, I am not... I don't love [inaudible 01:11:05] got TV, but we had rented Barbie for the kids. That one, probably the last movie.
turns.zh: 天哪，我不……我不喜欢电视节目，不过我们给孩子们租了《芭比》。这部可能是我最近看的最后一部电影了。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Oh wow.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.en: Yeah, you can watch it at home. But it's not cheap. I think it's like 20 bucks in the US.
turns.zh: 是啊，可以在家看。但不便宜。我记得美国要20美元。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Oh geez.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite interview question you like to ask candidates when you're interviewing them?
turns.zh: 面试时，你最喜欢问候选人的一个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, so I only ask two. I got down to asking just two questions over time. The first one's probably my favorite, which is, what is it that most frustrates you about... Instead of why you're leaving, what frustrates you the most about where you're working right now? And this is as people always tell you why they want to join Wise, or join whatever company you're coming to, and that's not that interesting. But what's interesting, trying to figure out, is what they're running away from. And usually there's something broken there, that's really wound them up. But what's more interesting is they've been unable to fix it. And so, in asking this question, and probing, you kind of get quite good at getting a sense of what is their limit, what's the thing they found, and what did they get stuck with? And you kind of think, "Okay, you're going to run into that here every day, every week? Or... You should be fine." And that's kind of why I ask that question.
turns.zh: 是啊，我只问两个问题。随着时间推移，我只问两个问题。第一个是我最喜欢的，就是“最让你沮丧的是什么？” 而不是“你为什么离职”，或者“你为什么想加入Wise或其他公司”，那些没意思。更有意思的是试图弄清楚他们在逃避什么。通常那里有某个问题，真的让他们抓狂。但更有意思的是他们没能解决它。所以问这个问题，深入探讨，你就能很好地了解他们的极限、他们发现了什么、又被什么困住了。然后你会想，“好吧，你每天、每周都会遇到这些问题？还是……你应该没事的。” 这就是我问这个问题的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.en: I recently switched to Arc Browser.
turns.zh: 我最近换用了Arc浏览器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I use.
turns.zh: 这就是我常用的浏览器。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: And yeah, the onboarding flow was mind-blowingly good.
turns.zh: 没错，新用户引导流程简直太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly how I felt. I had to tweet about it. It's like, [inaudible 01:12:41].
turns.zh: 我完全赞同。我甚至专门为此发了推特。简直太棒了，[听不清 01:12:41]。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: Yeah, I sent it to my onboarding team, and everyone. And what I loved about it is, it's clearly like if you could try to use Arc with the same way you use Chrome, you just get really frustrated. But if you use it the way they want you to use, it'd be amazing. So, for figuring out how to get people to engage with, you need to use this fundamentally differently. They manage to almost get me to use it the right way. Still struggling a little bit with it, but that I thought was really clever.
turns.zh: 是的，我把它分享给了我的新用户引导团队，还有所有人。最让我感触的是，显然如果你试图用和使用Chrome一样的方式来用Arc，肯定会很沮丧。但如果你按照他们的引导方式使用，那简直太棒了。所以，要想让用户真正参与进来，就必须用完全不同的方式来设计。他们成功地让我几乎学会了正确的使用方法。虽然我现在还有点不太适应，但我觉得这真的很聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome choice. We had Josh, the CEO of the Browser Company of New York, it's called, on the podcast. And if you're interested in learning about Arc's story, definitely check out that episode. All right, next question. What is a favorite life motto that you like to repeat most to yourself, that you like to share? Anything come to mind?
turns.zh: 很棒的选择。我们邀请了纽约浏览器公司的首席执行官乔希上播客。如果你有兴趣了解Arc的故事，欢迎去听那期节目。好的，下一个问题。你最喜欢、最常对自己说、最乐意分享的人生格言是什么？有没有什么特别的想法？

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: The thing that defines success is the speed at which you pick yourself up.
turns.zh: 定义成功的关键在于你能多快振作起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这句话了。

turns.speaker: Nilan Peiris
turns.en: And that's the thing that I hold onto most, because you get knocked a lot, high growth company, and it's obviously quite... Obviously knocks you, when someone says no to an offer, when somebody leaves the company, when a product doesn't work as you think it should, when you get pushback from a partner. But yeah, if you lose four hours spinning around it, or you trying and figure out, "Okay, this happened, how do I move forward?" And just learning how to shorten that time has probably been one of the most important journeys for me.
turns.zh: 这是我最坚持的信念，因为在高增长公司里，你会经常遭遇挫折。当有人拒绝你的提议、有人离职、产品不如预期、合作伙伴反对时，这些都会带来打击。但如果你为此浪费四小时纠结，或者试图找出解决办法——比如“好吧，这种情况发生了，我该如何前进？”——学会缩短这个过程，可能是对我最重要的成长经历。
